meta.title: MCP Question Bank — Chapter 7: Authorization (multi-select)
meta.revision: v2.1 (curated 2026-09-12, 200 items, verified against the 2026-07-28 specification)

questions.question: Which status/condition pairings are correct for a protected MCP server? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: 401 for a missing, invalid or expired token
403 for a token issued for a different MCP server
403 for a valid token whose scopes are insufficient
429 for a client that has exceeded its step-up retry limit

questions.explanation: The spec's table is 401 unauthorized, 403 forbidden (invalid scopes or insufficient permissions), 400 bad request. A wrong-audience token is an invalid token, so 401. Retry limits are client-side behaviour, not a defined server response.

questions.question: Which requirements does the authorization spec place on discovery? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Clients MUST support both metadata discovery mechanisms
MCP servers MUST host their own authorization server at the same origin
Authorization servers MUST provide RFC 8414 metadata, OIDC Discovery, or both
Clients MUST cache the discovery documents for the lifetime of the token
MCP servers MUST implement OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728)

questions.explanation: A, B and C are explicit requirements. Caching policy is not mandated, and the authorization server may be hosted with the resource server or be an entirely separate entity.

questions.question: Which token-handling rules does the spec state? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: An MCP server calling an upstream API must obtain its own token for that API
Clients MUST store refresh tokens in the same store as the user's password manager
MCP servers MAY forward the client's token upstream if the audience allows it
Refresh tokens MUST be rotated for public clients
Authorization servers SHOULD issue short-lived access tokens

questions.explanation: Short-lived tokens and refresh-token rotation for public clients are explicit; token passthrough is explicitly forbidden, so an MCP server acting as a client upstream uses a separate token from the upstream authorization server.
